meta.titre: Exodus and Moses: from slavery in Egypt to the covenant at Sinai
meta.sous_theme: The call, the deliverance, the wilderness journey and the role of people around Moses
tags: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Religious Studies past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: Songs and sermons in many Cameroonian churches return to the story of the Exodus: a people who escape slavery, cross the sea, are fed in the wilderness and receive God's law. It is also a regular topic at the GCE, because it supplies both short factual questions (where, who, which event) and essay questions on the persons around Moses. To score well you need the events in the correct order, and the skill of explaining why each person or event mattered.

items: The descendants of Jacob, also called Israel, settled in Egypt in the time of Joseph.
A covenant is a solemn agreement between God and a people.
Pharaoh was the title of the king of Egypt.

sections.titre: The life of Moses and the events of the Exodus
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Moses: birth, flight and call
- Moses was born to a Hebrew family when Pharaoh had ordered Hebrew baby boys to be killed. He was hidden in a basket among the reeds of the Nile, found by Pharaoh's daughter and brought up in the royal household.
- As an adult he killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew and fled to Midian. There he met Jethro, the priest of Midian, who gave him hospitality, and he married Jethro's daughter Zipporah and worked as a shepherd.
- At the burning bush on Mount Horeb (Sinai) God called Moses to bring the Israelites out of Egypt. Moses protested that he was not a good speaker, so his brother Aaron was appointed to speak for him (Exodus 3 and 4).

### From Egypt to Sinai
| Event | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| The plagues and the Passover (Exodus 12) | After a series of plagues, the last being the death of the firstborn, the Israelites marked their doors with the blood of a lamb and ate a hurried meal; Pharaoh let them go. | Jews still celebrate Passover as the festival of liberation. |
| The Red Sea (Exodus 14) | Pharaoh's army pursued them, so the Israelites were trapped between the sea and the Egyptians. Moses told them not to fear and to stand firm; the sea was divided, they crossed and the pursuing Egyptians were drowned. | It shows God as deliverer and ends the threat from Egypt. |
| The wilderness (Exodus 15 to 17) | After the crossing the people's first complaint was at Marah, where the water was bitter; later came the manna and the quails, water from the rock and the battle against the Amalekites at Rephidim. | The people depend on God and test the leadership of Moses. |
| Jethro's visit (Exodus 18) | Jethro came to the camp, rejoiced at the deliverance and advised Moses to appoint capable men as judges over groups of people, leaving only the hardest cases to Moses. | It introduces shared leadership and a system of justice. |
| Sinai (Exodus 19 to 32) | The covenant was made, the Ten Commandments given, and in the absence of Moses the people made the golden calf. | It defines Israel as the people of the covenant. |

Moses led the people for forty years in the wilderness but died before they entered Canaan; Joshua then led them in.

### Answering 'examine the role of...'
Identify the person, narrate their actions briefly, then explain the effect on Moses and on the Israelites and give a judgement of importance.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to examine or assess the role of Aaron, Jethro or another person.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use three paragraphs: what the person did (with episodes), how this helped Moses personally and the people as a whole, and a judgement on how important the person was. Include a limitation where the account shows one, such as Aaron making the golden calf.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked about the Red Sea crossing, the plagues or the Passover.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give the situation before, the event, the result, and the religious meaning. Keep the order: plagues and Passover, then the Red Sea, then the wilderness, then Sinai.

sections.enonce_markdown: Assess the importance of Aaron in the Exodus story. (15 marks)

etapes.justification: 'Assess' needs a judgement of importance supported by evidence, and a balanced view.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The answer must show Aaron's contributions and also his limitations.

etapes.justification: Evidence has to come from the narrative.
etapes.resultat_markdown: He spoke for Moses before Pharaoh, supported him at Rephidim, was consecrated first high priest, and made the golden calf.

etapes.action: Group the evidence into a plan.
etapes.justification: Grouping gives paragraphs rather than a list.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Paragraph 1: spokesman. Paragraph 2: support in the wilderness. Paragraph 3: priesthood. Paragraph 4: failure at Sinai.

etapes.action: Develop each paragraph with its effect.
etapes.resultat_markdown: As spokesman he made up for Moses' reluctance; at Rephidim he and Hur held up the arms of Moses during the battle with the Amalekites; as high priest he led the worship at the tabernacle.
Aaron was important as helper and priest, although his part in the golden calf shows weakness.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer.** Aaron was an important figure, though not a flawless one. When Moses doubted his ability to speak, God appointed Aaron, his brother, as spokesman, so Aaron stood with Moses before Pharaoh. In the wilderness he supported Moses at Rephidim, where he and Hur held up the arms of Moses during the battle with the Amalekites. He was later consecrated as the first high priest and so began the Israelite priesthood. His importance is limited by his failure at Sinai, when he made the golden calf at the demand of the people while Moses was on the mountain. In conclusion, Aaron was a vital helper and the founder of the priesthood, although his weakness shows that the leadership of Moses was unique.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that Moses led the Israelites into Canaan.
items.pourquoi_faux: Moses died before entering the land; Joshua led the people in.
items.correction_markdown: Write that Moses led them to the edge of Canaan and that Joshua succeeded him.

items.erreur_markdown: Placing the giving of the Ten Commandments before the crossing of the Red Sea.
items.pourquoi_faux: The Exodus narrative runs from plagues and Passover to the Red Sea, the wilderness and then Sinai.
items.correction_markdown: Keep the order: Passover, Red Sea, wilderness, Sinai.

items.erreur_markdown: Describing Jethro as an Egyptian or as an Israelite.
items.pourquoi_faux: Jethro was the priest of Midian and the father-in-law of Moses.
items.correction_markdown: Describe him as a Midianite priest.

items.erreur_markdown: Telling the story of the Exodus when the question says 'examine the role of' a person.
items.pourquoi_faux: A narrative without explanation does not show importance.
items.correction_markdown: Link each action of the person to its effect on Moses and the people, then give a judgement.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the brother of Moses who spoke for him before Pharaoh and the Midianite priest who became his father-in-law.
items.solution_markdown: The brother was **Aaron** and the priest was **Jethro**.

items.enonce_markdown: Describe what happened at Marah and at Rephidim during the journey in the wilderness. (8 marks)
items.solution_markdown: Marah: the people found only bitter water and complained to Moses; the water was made drinkable (up to 4 marks). Rephidim: the people were short of water and Moses was told to strike the rock, from which water came; the Amalekites also attacked, and the Israelites prevailed while Moses kept his arms raised with the help of Aaron and Hur (up to 4 marks). **Award 4 marks for each place.**

items.enonce_markdown: Discuss the importance of the Passover and the crossing of the Red Sea for the identity of the Israelites. (15 marks)
items.solution_markdown: Points: the Passover marked the end of slavery, and Jews still remember it each year; the crossing ended the Egyptian threat and showed God as deliverer; the later covenant at Sinai is based on this deliverance, since the Ten Commandments begin by recalling that God brought the people out of Egypt; they formed a common memory that bound the tribes as one people. Evaluation: the people's repeated complaints show that the memory did not at once give them faith. **Conclusion: these two events gave Israel its founding memory and its sense of being a people chosen for a covenant.** Award marks for accurate narrative, explanation of significance and a reasoned conclusion.

items_markdown: Moses was raised in Pharaoh's household, fled to Midian, married the daughter of the priest Jethro, and was called at the burning bush.
Aaron was Moses' brother and spokesman and became the first high priest.
Sequence: plagues and Passover, the Red Sea, the wilderness (Marah, manna, Rephidim), Jethro's advice, Sinai.
At the Red Sea the Israelites were trapped between the sea and the pursuing Egyptians.
Jethro advised Moses to share the work of judging among capable men.
'Examine' and 'assess' need explanation of importance and a judgement, not a narrative alone.
